title: Cells and Organs of the Immune System
subtitle: Hematopoietic lineages, antigen-presenting cells, and lymphoid organization.
author: Tikrit University · College of Medicine · Microbiology Department

blocks.title: Immune cells: origin and functional grouping

blocks.text: Immune cells arise from pluripotent hematopoietic stem cells in bone marrow. Growth factors and cytokines direct differentiation into lymphoid and myeloid lineages. Cell size, nuclear shape, cytoplasmic granules, surface markers, tissue distribution, and immune function distinguish the mature populations.

blocks.title: Learning objectives
items: Compare granulocytes, monocytes, macrophages, and dendritic cells
Locate lymphocyte maturation in primary lymphoid organs
Relate lymph-node and splenic compartments to immune function

blocks.title: Lymphoid cells
rows: Recognizes native antigen through surface immunoglobulin; differentiates into plasma and memory cells
Recognizes peptide presented by MHC class II
Recognizes peptide presented by MHC class I
Produces a faster and stronger secondary response
Recognizes cellular abnormality without antigen-specific receptors

steps.title: Activation
steps.description: Appropriate antigen and helper signals stimulate the B cell.

steps.title: Memory formation
steps.description: Long-lived cells support a rapid secondary response.

blocks.title: Granulocytes and mast cells
rows: Rapid phagocytosis and killing in acute inflammation
Defense against parasites and participation in allergy
Immediate hypersensitivity, vascular change, and inflammatory recruitment

blocks.title: Monocytes, macrophages, and dendritic cells
rows: 12–20 µm; horseshoe- or kidney-shaped nucleus; cytoplasmic granules and lysosomes; nondividing in blood
Migrates into tissue and differentiates into macrophages
Free or fixed tissue phagocyte within the mononuclear phagocyte system
Phagocytosis, microbial killing, debris removal, cytokine release, tissue repair, and MHC II antigen presentation
Highly effective antigen-presenting cell; includes epidermal Langerhans cells
Captures antigen, activates CD4 and CD8 T cells, and produces IL-12 that promotes TH1 responses

steps.title: Circulating monocyte
steps.description: A nondividing blood cell carries lysosomes and cytoplasmic granules.

steps.title: Local defense
steps.description: The macrophage phagocytoses, presents antigen, releases cytokines, and supports repair.

blocks.title: Specialized tissue phagocytes
rows: Removes blood-borne material, including gut-derived antigen

blocks.title: Bone marrow and thymus
rows: Generates hematopoietic cells; supports B-cell development and central tolerance; releases T-cell progenitors to the thymus
Fetal liver is a major prenatal site; after birth marrow predominates; after puberty hematopoiesis is concentrated in the axial skeleton
Supports antigen-independent T-cell proliferation, selection, maturation, and central tolerance
Arises from third and fourth pharyngeal pouches; develops by the third embryonic month; active at birth; maximal near puberty; later involutes; bilobed above the heart

steps.title: Bone-marrow progenitor
steps.description: A lymphoid precursor enters the circulation.

steps.title: Thymic cortex
steps.description: Immature T cells proliferate and undergo selection.

steps.title: Thymic medulla
steps.description: Surviving cells continue maturation and tolerance selection.

steps.title: Mature naïve T cell
steps.description: Cells leave for secondary lymphoid tissues without prior foreign-antigen exposure.

blocks.title: Thymic mediators and competence
blocks.text: Thymopoietin and thymosins support T-cell development. Neonatal thymectomy impairs immune competence because mature T-cell populations have not yet been established.

blocks.title: Lymph-node organization
rows: B-cell follicles; germinal centers after activation
T cells and interdigitating dendritic cells
T cells, B cells, plasma cells, and macrophages
Antibody secretion, filtration, and effector-cell organization

steps.title: Lymph-borne antigen arrives
steps.description: Afferent lymph carries antigen and antigen-presenting cells.

steps.title: Regional capture
steps.description: Macrophages and dendritic cells sample material.

steps.title: Compartmental activation
steps.description: B cells respond in follicles; T cells respond in the paracortex.

steps.title: Effector generation
steps.description: Plasma cells, activated lymphocytes, and memory cells develop.

steps.title: Egress
steps.description: Cells and antibodies leave through efferent lymph.

blocks.title: Splenic compartments
rows: B cells with mantle, marginal, and germinal-center regions
Sinusoids, macrophages, red blood cells, and fewer lymphocytes
Filters blood and removes old or damaged blood cells

blocks.title: Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue
rows: Diffuse and organized lymphoid tissue at mucosal surfaces
Rapid response at major portals of entry
Tonsils, adenoids, appendix, and Peyer patches

blocks.title: Integrated cell–organ map
rows: Source of lymphoid and myeloid lineages
Bone marrow; follicles in secondary organs
Filters lymph and organizes regional responses
Filters blood and organizes blood-borne antigen responses

exam.title: Immune cells and organs exam
exam.instructions: Answer every question. Submit once to receive a score, correct answers, and explanations.

questions.prompt: Which cell recognizes peptide presented by MHC class II?
questions.explanation: CD4 T cells recognize peptide–MHC II complexes.

questions.prompt: Which cell recognizes peptide presented by MHC class I?
questions.explanation: CD8 T cells recognize peptide–MHC I complexes.

questions.prompt: A circulating monocyte differentiates into a tissue _____.
questions.explanation: Tissue migration and differentiation generate macrophages.

questions.prompt: How many principal hematopoietic lineages are described?
questions.explanation: The major lineages are lymphoid and myeloid.

questions.prompt: Match each specialized phagocyte to its location.
questions.explanation: These are tissue-adapted members of the mononuclear phagocyte system.

questions.history: A newborn undergoes thymectomy before mature T-cell populations are established.

questions.prompt: Where are B-cell follicles located in a lymph node?
Which lymph-node region is rich in T cells and interdigitating dendritic cells?
questions.explanation: The paracortex is the T-cell zone.

questions.prompt: The T-cell sheath around a splenic central arteriole is the _____.
questions.explanation: PALS is the periarteriolar lymphoid sheath.

questions.prompt: Match each splenic region to its dominant function.
questions.explanation: The spleen separates immune activation from blood filtration across these compartments.

questions.history: A blood-borne encapsulated organism reaches a lymphoid organ that filters blood and removes old erythrocytes.
questions.explanation: The spleen filters blood and mounts responses to blood-borne antigen.

questions.prompt: Which dendritic-cell cytokine promotes TH1 responses?
How many embryonic pharyngeal pouch levels contribute to the thymus?
questions.explanation: The third and fourth pharyngeal pouches contribute.

questions.prompt: Epidermal dendritic cells are called _____ cells.
questions.explanation: Langerhans cells are epidermal dendritic cells.
The names indicate their anatomical associations.

questions.history: A lymph-node biopsy shows an expanded germinal center.
questions.prompt: Which cell population is primarily proliferating there?
questions.explanation: Germinal centers are sites of activated B-cell proliferation and differentiation.

questions.prompt: Which cell is most associated with antiparasitic defense?
questions.explanation: Eosinophils participate prominently in antiparasitic responses.

questions.prompt: After puberty, hematopoiesis becomes concentrated mainly in the _____ skeleton.
questions.explanation: Active marrow becomes concentrated in the axial skeleton.
